Dylan's Journey: From Autism to the Stage

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When Dylan Kritzinger was diagnosed with Autism at age 8, doctors said he'd never function independently, never speak a full sentence or even dress himself, but now he's about to graduate matric!

Unique Selling Point:
What it's like to have Autism: Dylan's journey...

I have video of him speaking...


Dylan turned 19 on November 2029 and is currently completing his final year at Pecanwood College – he is 2 years behind his peers on an academic level due to a host of learning difficulties.

It was between the ages 18 months to 2 years when I felt that Dylan was not reaching milestones and was in fact regressing. We consulted with many specialists and experts over the next few years - GP’s, Pediatricians, Neurologists, Psychologists, Psychometrists, AS Specialists, Developmental Delay Experts, Remedial Therapists, Occupational Therapists, Speech & Language Therapists, Headmasters & Teachers, and received various diagnoses from across the globe including Speech Apraxia & Severe Developmental Delay, Petit Mal Seizures, ADD and Dyslexia to name a few.

His biological father and I got divorced when Dylan was 3½ years. old. We kept an amicable relationship and Dylan enjoyed visiting his dad every second weekend.

Between the ages 4yrs and 10yrs, Dylan attended 8 different schools, all of which were 40+km away from home (and so we spent a large portion of our days traveling backwards and forwards with no social interaction with classmates after school). Most of these schools were not prepared or equipped to educate Dylan and we were asked to leave school and find a place “more suitable” after just a few months in most instances. With virtually no verbal skills still at the age of 7, it was challenging for teachers to communicate with Dylan and vice versa. Dylan was, at this stage, frustrated, unhappy, anxious, and often ran out of his classroom to find a quiet space. Over these 6 years, he was withdrawn and lacked the confidence to leave my side in the mornings – it was heart-breaking dropping him at school. He hardly showed emotion to others and was never excited about his day - always anxious, always sad

It was just after Dylan’s 7th birthday that I was referred to yet another paediatric neurologist who came highly recommended. After waiting 8 months for an appointment, Dylan was diagnosed with Classic Autism on the high end of the spectrum within 15 minutes into the appointment. We were advised to place Dylan in a home for Autistic Children ASAP, where we could visit or take him home over the weekends. The specialist stated that - without the help of trained medical professionals & therapists. We were devastated, but putting my son in a home was not an option for me. I had lost my eldest boy to cancer only a few years prior, and couldn’t imagine not having Dylan with me every day – so I discarded the expert advice and set about prioritizing less but more effective therapies and treatments to cope with immediate challenges, making Dylan’s life more comfortable and less anxious. At this point I was fully aware of what Autism was and was not in denial – I simply decided to not use the label and rather focus on one day peaceful and happy day at a time.

One day, at the age of 8 yrs. and 4 mos., Dylan spoke a full and clear sentence on our way home from school. It was one of the happiest days of both our lives and the start of a whole new journey. We continued having short but rapidly improving conversations, only in the car, and only when it was just the 2 of us for some time. He then started conversing with more people and at the age of 10 had the vocabulary of a 5-year-old. At this point I met one of the most dedicated and compassionate teachers ever at our local mainstream school, who was incredibly passionate about children with learning difficulties. Dylan was not accepted into the school after completing the standard assessment test, but Mrs. Nadia Prinsloo insisted that she would give Dylan a chance in her bridging class. He thrived from day 1 given the opportunity to be treated like any other learner and of course being at school so close to home, not spending hours on the road and participating in sports for the first time. Dylan started at a Grade 00 level in the bridging class and by the end of the year completed the Grade 2 syllabus.

During the same year Dylan went on School Camp for 2 nights, leaving the “safety” of home for the first time ever. He returned happy and relaxed - a different child having made friends (still best friends 10 years later), building confidence and feeling a strong sense of belonging in the school and among his peers. He also attended Speech and Drama lessons at the Barnyard Theatre in Rivonia twice a week and steadily improved his confidence levels. It was during this time I believe Dylan’s love for the stage begun. Expressing himself in front of audiences became a lot easier than having one-on-one conversations, and he continued to participate in any opportunity at school thereafter – from poetry festivals, prepared speeches and school concerts in junior phase to selecting Drama as a subject from Grade 10 onwards.

Dylan spent 2 years in the bridging class before he moved on to mainstream Grade 5, and with the assistance of a facilitator, passed his junior school grades each year. He became a proud, dedicated, loyal, independent and responsible boy almost overnight.



Summary:
Tragically at the end of Dylan’s Grade 6 year, his dad passed away in a car accident at the age of 51. A year later, his grandfather who he confided in, and spent may afternoons with, also unexpectedly passed on after having suffered a major heart attack. Dylan’s grandpa Kritzinger also passed away recently, and Dylan was the only person delivering a eulogy at the memorial service – incredibly touching, well prepared and with great confidence.

Amidst his personal losses and increasing academic pressure, Dylan however continued to show remarkable progress in his Grade 7 year. His marks improved significantly term-on-term and he gained great confidence in doing so.

He was selected as a Leader at the end of the year – an achievement that once again had an amazing effect on his self-esteem.

In 2016, during final assembly of junior school, Dylan was given the Headmaster’s Award by the late Mr Nigel Sloane with the following citation:





Further information:
“Today is the first time in many years the Headmaster’s Award has been presented. It recognises someone who has shone in the face of adversity. Someone who has shown true grit and determination to achieve their goals. This it is awarded to a young man who has faced many challenges and yet has never given up. A young man who has soldiered on. In spite of his barriers and learning challenges, he has gained the recognition of staff, peers and pupils. This was highlighted by him being elected as a Grade 7 school leader. This worthy recipient is Dylan Kritzinger.”



Dylan and I have always been extremely close. In the early days I had to read his mind and speak for him. I was the only person he made eye-contact with, hugged or held hands with. He is now an affectionate young man, generous with hugs and particularly in tune with the moods of those around him, and we now have long talks about life, people, fears, goals, his future and his passions.

Once, in his first high school year, said he knew he was not “normal” and asked that I explain to him one day why he is so “different” to everyone else and why he doesn’t always “fit in”. I said that I had stacks of documents at the office with every bit of detail filed for when he was ready. He did not mention this again until April 2018 (age 17), when I took him to my office on a quiet Sunday afternoon and we spent almost 4 hours reliving his history he could not remember much of. We cried and laughed while I told stories of schools, teachers, awkward moments, doctors and therapists and showed drawings and school reports from years ago. When I finally got to the official report diagnosing him with Autism, we read over the standard check list for autistic traits. Dylan himself checked over the list. He said he didn’t fit into most of the check boxes and that the specialist must have been mistaken. He was however very concerned about me and how it all affected my life. We hugged, cried some more – I told him how immensely proud I was to be given such a special person to share a life with, and that I had learned so much from him.

From this day onwards Dylan never asked about being “different” again, but instead started talking about sharing his journey with others. His message is one of hope and determination and hard work, always finding a way around a challenge and not believing in the labels that society like to brand us all with. He has worked extremely hard at Drama and participated in a number of plays – one of which was chosen to perform at TUKS in 2019.

Dylan received half colours for Drama at the end of Grade 10 – again an unusually early achievement in high school. He was also selected to play first team rugby in 2020 and 2021.

He is passionate about sharing his inspirational story to audiences and motivate others.

Dylan was accepted to start a Diploma in Wildlife Conservation at Bushwise College in Hoedspruit in 2022, to ultimately work with wild animals in distress such as at an orphanage or rehabilitation facility

Dylan is currently finishing matric at Pecanwood College having spent most of 2020 and a large part of 2021 navigating his education online. He was selected as a member of the RDI (Respect, Diversity and Inclusion) Committee at the end of his Grade 11 year which he serves passionately, displaying a refreshingly liberal approach.

He successfully passed his driver’s licence in July 2021 at first attempt and is well on his way to be 100% inde






Dylan speaks fairly well when prepared and is able to express his feelings but has trouble keeping eye contact. His reading and writing has improved over time but still needs assistance with explaining paragraphs and questions when reading (dyslexia). We applied for a number of academic concessions a few years ago. He works with a facilitator at school, a scribe during exams, extra exam time, 6 subjects only, many additional extra lessons outside of school. Retention is a challenge, yet he is able to memorise lengthy drama scripts and never forgets them.
He has a passion for animals in distress and will be studying wildlife in Hoedspruit next year. He just passed his driver’s licence and is currently preparing for prelim exams
There are a number of exceptionally compassionate teachers and an educational psychologist who have walked this journey with our family for years that can be contacted for more information
Below is a link to one of his recent drama performances and a note from his drama teacher


https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1QWqhu4IAyt9BUPkSu23blKGfSVBYo_k5?usp=sharing


“This from the movie where Zac Efron plays Ted Bundy. I felt it was a true testament to how far Dylan came. I met him in Grade 8 and he struggled to look you in the eye, or verbalise a sentence. Now, here he is playing Ted Bundy to a ‘T’”

He said this child, unfortunately, is highly autistic, most likely very low functioning. We need to consider putting him in a home he most likely will never speak properly, dress himself

I had lost a child before Dylan was born to brain cancer and fighting for a child's life is very different to fighting a label like this.

We had spent a lot of time in the car Travelling to different schools a lot. I did ask, how was your day? And suddenly he answered to me, He said, I had a good day mom.

I did.

In the beginning that he didn't pass the entrance exam. and I fought to have him and I got him. And I took Dylan into my bridging class. And I said, Look at me. I touched his hand. I said, I look at me.And he actually looked at me and he started doing what I told him to do. Dylan didn't know how to do most things. He couldn't put colors together. He didn't recognise his own name.
It wasn’t easy, Dylan had to painstakingly pass several years of school during his bridging class, but his strong support system helped him overcome his learning barriers, and to everyone's amazement after two years he joined mainstream classes.
Making friends wasn’t easy, until he met neighbour Paige Smilie.
Now I've been told you were like the bodyguard?
Yes, I was. (can we cover the cut and take out um)
Were you protecting him?
I just didn't want him to go through things that. People would normally go through those younger days if you were different, people would point it out and kids can be mean.
And he's quite time specific, time conscious?
Yes.So we are reminded very often that flexibility is not in his vocab. He does not do flexibility when we say we leaving at seven minutes to eight, Dylan will be ready at seven minutes to eight.
He's going to pass matric. He's finishing it in one year. I think of the doctors they saw him and diagnosed him have to see him now.
I don't think they will even recognize this child.
A label Dylan doesn’t mind is actor. And helping him perform is Drama teacher Tania van der Wyver.
you're talking about a young man who couldn't look you in the eye a few years ago.
Exactly. And that's how much he's grown. And I think a big thing for Dylan, especially when it comes to drama and performing, is the fact that he gets to let go.he likes things that are right and that are wrong. And the moment that he can play a character like that, he gets to put himself in someone else's shoes.
His acting partner is Hannah Brown.
I enjoy it because I feel like we both help each other. I like to help Dylan become more into the piece, And he he's also very good at making sure I am practicing


ACTING BLEEP the bullshit lol they loved the bullshit

So it definitely like it just to feel change different person, just to have a break with like my personality
what annoys you or upsets you about life, society, people?
simply putting judgments on people and also people's differences
And that may have been what inspired him to help start a school committee to make students like Hannah feel more accepted.
we simply try to make trying to be like trying to make some of the students equal to the school.
From a young age, I've been very masculine presenting in the way I present myself. I've got the guys uniform on. I'm also gay, so that's something society deems is different.

Dylan: So it was a bit stressful and was scary the same time. I was tearful when I got my letter. I was ready to go home.
DYLAN READS LETTER
After reading the letter decided, gotta keep going.
He recently passed his drivers test, first time,

Yes, for sure. it just shows that it is possible to prove people wrong.
in those quiet moments when you want to be alone, what goes through your mind
like simply by how different I am and like and also think about my future goal would be? And one of your goals is to go to a Bush College next year?
yes to become a game ranger and then later on on a game lodge and also make it the famous well-known game reserve by its conservation.
Do you feel a sense of freedom when you're in the bush?
Yes, it's like very peaceful and our own. To be honest, I don't feel much. And I feel different in the bush
Derek: It seems that a lot of your success Has revolved around proving other people wrong.
Yes, for sure. it just shows that it is possible to prove people wrong.
I think there are a lot of lessons to be learnt here especially in the definition of success?
I think as a family, we have never really wanted our children necessarily to go and build empires. they need to find a place where they can build a happy life, and inspire people.

BUT ITS NOT ABOUT MEDICAL DISCOVERIES...ITS ABOUT ONE YOUNG MANS JOURNEY ALONG WITH THE FAMILY. There are few statistics on Autism in South Africa however it affects 1-2% of the world's population. I had lost a child before Dylan was born to brain cancer and fighting for a child's life is very different to fighting a label like this. Dylan loves nature, and after he’d interacted with farm animals at school one day he had a breakthrough with his communication barrier We had spent a lot of time in the car Travelling to different schools a lot. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When Dylan Kritzinger was diagnosed with Autism at age 8, doctors said he'd never function independently, never speak a full sentence or even dress himself, but now he's about to graduate matric!
metadata.Unique Selling Point: What it's like to have Autism: Dylan's journey... I have video of him speaking... Dylan turned 19 on November 2029 and is currently completing his final year at Pecanwood College – he is 2 years behind his peers on an academic level due to a host of learning difficulties. It was between the ages 18 months to 2 years when I felt that Dylan was not reaching milestones and was in fact regressing. We consulted with many specialists and experts over the next few years - GP’s, Pediatricians, Neurologists, Psychologists, Psychometrists, AS Specialists, Developmental Delay Experts, Remedial Therapists, Occupational Therapists, Speech & Language Therapists, Headmasters & Teachers, and received various diagnoses from across the globe including Speech Apraxia & Severe Developmental Delay, Petit Mal Seizures, ADD and Dyslexia to name a few. His biological father and I got divorced when Dylan was 3½ years. old. We kept an amicable relationship and Dylan enjoyed visiting his dad every second weekend. Between the ages 4yrs and 10yrs, Dylan attended 8 different schools, all of which were 40+km away from home (and so we spent a large portion of our days traveling backwards and forwards with no social interaction with classmates after school). Most of these schools were not prepared or equipped to educate Dylan and we were asked to leave school and find a place “more suitable” after just a few months in most instances. With virtually no verbal skills still at the age of 7, it was challenging for teachers to communicate with Dylan and vice versa. Dylan was, at this stage, frustrated, unhappy, anxious, and often ran out of his classroom to find a quiet space. Over these 6 years, he was withdrawn and lacked the confidence to leave my side in the mornings – it was heart-breaking dropping him at school. He hardly showed emotion to others and was never excited about his day - always anxious, always sad It was just after Dylan’s 7th birthday that I was referred to yet another paediatric neurologist who came highly recommended. After waiting 8 months for an appointment, Dylan was diagnosed with Classic Autism on the high end of the spectrum within 15 minutes into the appointment. We were advised to place Dylan in a home for Autistic Children ASAP, where we could visit or take him home over the weekends. The specialist stated that - without the help of trained medical professionals & therapists. We were devastated, but putting my son in a home was not an option for me. I had lost my eldest boy to cancer only a few years prior, and couldn’t imagine not having Dylan with me every day – so I discarded the expert advice and set about prioritizing less but more effective therapies and treatments to cope with immediate challenges, making Dylan’s life more comfortable and less anxious. At this point I was fully aware of what Autism was and was not in denial – I simply decided to not use the label and rather focus on one day peaceful and happy day at a time. One day, at the age of 8 yrs. and 4 mos., Dylan spoke a full and clear sentence on our way home from school. It was one of the happiest days of both our lives and the start of a whole new journey. We continued having short but rapidly improving conversations, only in the car, and only when it was just the 2 of us for some time. He then started conversing with more people and at the age of 10 had the vocabulary of a 5-year-old. At this point I met one of the most dedicated and compassionate teachers ever at our local mainstream school, who was incredibly passionate about children with learning difficulties. Dylan was not accepted into the school after completing the standard assessment test, but Mrs. Nadia Prinsloo insisted that she would give Dylan a chance in her bridging class. He thrived from day 1 given the opportunity to be treated like any other learner and of course being at school so close to home, not spending hours on the road and participating in sports for the first time. Dylan started at a Grade 00 level in the bridging class and by the end of the year completed the Grade 2 syllabus. During the same year Dylan went on School Camp for 2 nights, leaving the “safety” of home for the first time ever. He returned happy and relaxed - a different child having made friends (still best friends 10 years later), building confidence and feeling a strong sense of belonging in the school and among his peers. He also attended Speech and Drama lessons at the Barnyard Theatre in Rivonia twice a week and steadily improved his confidence levels. It was during this time I believe Dylan’s love for the stage begun. Expressing himself in front of audiences became a lot easier than having one-on-one conversations, and he continued to participate in any opportunity at school thereafter – from poetry festivals, prepared speeches and school concerts in junior phase to selecting Drama as a subject from Grade 10 onwards. Dylan spent 2 years in the bridging class before he moved on to mainstream Grade 5, and with the assistance of a facilitator, passed his junior school grades each year. He became a proud, dedicated, loyal, independent and responsible boy almost overnight.
metadata.Summary: Tragically at the end of Dylan’s Grade 6 year, his dad passed away in a car accident at the age of 51. A year later, his grandfather who he confided in, and spent may afternoons with, also unexpectedly passed on after having suffered a major heart attack. Dylan’s grandpa Kritzinger also passed away recently, and Dylan was the only person delivering a eulogy at the memorial service – incredibly touching, well prepared and with great confidence. Amidst his personal losses and increasing academic pressure, Dylan however continued to show remarkable progress in his Grade 7 year. His marks improved significantly term-on-term and he gained great confidence in doing so. He was selected as a Leader at the end of the year – an achievement that once again had an amazing effect on his self-esteem. In 2016, during final assembly of junior school, Dylan was given the Headmaster’s Award by the late Mr Nigel Sloane with the following citation:
metadata.Further information: “Today is the first time in many years the Headmaster’s Award has been presented. It recognises someone who has shone in the face of adversity. Someone who has shown true grit and determination to achieve their goals. This it is awarded to a young man who has faced many challenges and yet has never given up. A young man who has soldiered on. In spite of his barriers and learning challenges, he has gained the recognition of staff, peers and pupils. This was highlighted by him being elected as a Grade 7 school leader. This worthy recipient is Dylan Kritzinger.” Dylan and I have always been extremely close. In the early days I had to read his mind and speak for him. I was the only person he made eye-contact with, hugged or held hands with. He is now an affectionate young man, generous with hugs and particularly in tune with the moods of those around him, and we now have long talks about life, people, fears, goals, his future and his passions. Once, in his first high school year, said he knew he was not “normal” and asked that I explain to him one day why he is so “different” to everyone else and why he doesn’t always “fit in”. I said that I had stacks of documents at the office with every bit of detail filed for when he was ready. He did not mention this again until April 2018 (age 17), when I took him to my office on a quiet Sunday afternoon and we spent almost 4 hours reliving his history he could not remember much of. We cried and laughed while I told stories of schools, teachers, awkward moments, doctors and therapists and showed drawings and school reports from years ago. When I finally got to the official report diagnosing him with Autism, we read over the standard check list for autistic traits. Dylan himself checked over the list. He said he didn’t fit into most of the check boxes and that the specialist must have been mistaken. He was however very concerned about me and how it all affected my life. We hugged, cried some more – I told him how immensely proud I was to be given such a special person to share a life with, and that I had learned so much from him. From this day onwards Dylan never asked about being “different” again, but instead started talking about sharing his journey with others. His message is one of hope and determination and hard work, always finding a way around a challenge and not believing in the labels that society like to brand us all with. He has worked extremely hard at Drama and participated in a number of plays – one of which was chosen to perform at TUKS in 2019. Dylan received half colours for Drama at the end of Grade 10 – again an unusually early achievement in high school. He was also selected to play first team rugby in 2020 and 2021. He is passionate about sharing his inspirational story to audiences and motivate others. Dylan was accepted to start a Diploma in Wildlife Conservation at Bushwise College in Hoedspruit in 2022, to ultimately work with wild animals in distress such as at an orphanage or rehabilitation facility Dylan is currently finishing matric at Pecanwood College having spent most of 2020 and a large part of 2021 navigating his education online. He was selected as a member of the RDI (Respect, Diversity and Inclusion) Committee at the end of his Grade 11 year which he serves passionately, displaying a refreshingly liberal approach. He successfully passed his driver’s licence in July 2021 at first attempt and is well on his way to be 100% inde Dylan speaks fairly well when prepared and is able to express his feelings but has trouble keeping eye contact. His reading and writing has improved over time but still needs assistance with explaining paragraphs and questions when reading (dyslexia). We applied for a number of academic concessions a few years ago. He works with a facilitator at school, a scribe during exams, extra exam time, 6 subjects only, many additional extra lessons outside of school. Retention is a challenge, yet he is able to memorise lengthy drama scripts and never forgets them. He has a passion for animals in distress and will be studying wildlife in Hoedspruit next year. He just passed his driver’s licence and is currently preparing for prelim exams There are a number of exceptionally compassionate teachers and an educational psychologist who have walked this journey with our family for years that can be contacted for more information Below is a link to one of his recent drama performances and a note from his drama teacher https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1QWqhu4IAyt9BUPkSu23blKGfSVBYo_k5?usp=sharing “This from the movie where Zac Efron plays Ted Bundy. I felt it was a true testament to how far Dylan came. I met him in Grade 8 and he struggled to look you in the eye, or verbalise a sentence. Now, here he is playing Ted Bundy to a ‘T’”
